summary: Defines the architecture of IPFIX, a way for network devices to watch traffic flows and send summaries of them to a collecting system. It describes the roles of the devices that measure and export flow data and the collector that receives it. It is an informational overview rather than the protocol itself.

plainLanguage.summary: Network operators need a standard way to count traffic and send the results to a central system. This memo describes the parts of that system: a device that watches packets and groups them into flows, a process that packs the summaries and sends them, and a collector that reads them. It sets out the overall design, while the exact rules for the protocol live in other documents.

questions: how does ip flow export architecture work
how does ip fix architecture work
subtitle: The blueprint for measuring network traffic as flows and exporting the results to a collector.

tldr.problem: Accounting, traffic engineering, intrusion detection and quality-of-service monitoring all need flow-based traffic measurements, and there was no standard architecture for exporting them.
tldr.mechanism: The design splits the job into observation points, metering processes that build Flow Records, an exporting process that sends them in IPFIX Messages, and a collecting process that decodes them using Templates.
tldr.outcome: It is an overview that sets requirements for recovery and security and points to RFC 5101 and RFC 5102 for the protocol and information model, and it was later updated by RFC 6183.

today: RFC 5470 is an Informational RFC published in March 2009 and has been updated by RFC 6183. It has not been obsoleted, and it describes the architecture while the protocol and information model are defined in RFC 5101 and RFC 5102.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Usage-based accounting, traffic profiling, traffic engineering, attack and intrusion detection, and quality-of-service monitoring all need flow-based IP traffic measurements. This memo defines the architecture for IP Flow Information eXport (IPFIX). Its main objectives are to describe the key components, at least IPFIX Devices and Collectors; to define the architectural requirements such as recovery and security; and to describe the characteristics of the protocol.

The work is split across several documents. The requirements are in RFC 3917, the protocol itself in RFC 5101, the information model in RFC 5102, and the applicability in RFC 5472. The RFC states plainly that the IPFIX system does not provide remote configuration of a device: implementors must supply their own way to configure an IPFIX device.
sections.plainLanguage: Many jobs need to know what kinds of traffic cross a network and how much of it there is. This memo draws the plan for the whole system: the device that watches, the process that sends, and the process that receives. It also warns that the system does not let you configure the device from a distance, so each implementor has to add that separately.

sections.title: Flows, Keys and Records
sections.content:
A Flow is a set of IP packets passing an Observation Point during a certain time interval, all sharing a set of common properties. Each property comes from packet header fields (such as the destination IP address), characteristics of the packet itself (such as the number of MPLS labels), or packet treatment (such as the next-hop address or the output interface). Each field used to define a flow is a Flow Key.

A Flow Record holds measured properties and usually characteristic properties of one flow. The memo's examples show how the choice of keys shapes the result: with the keys being source address, destination address and DSCP, the examples produce eight flows; masking the low bits of the addresses merges them into six; and a filter that fixes the key values reduces those to one.

An Observation Point is a place where packets can be observed, such as a line to which a probe is attached or a single router port. An Observation Domain is the largest set of Observation Points for which flow information can be aggregated by one Metering Process, and it carries an Observation Domain ID that is unique per Exporting Process.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is a group of packets that share the same distinguishing details, such as coming from the same address and going to the same place. A flow record is the tally sheet for one such group. A flow key is any one of the details used to sort packets into groups, and an observation point is the spot where the packets are seen.

sections.title: The Functional Blocks
sections.content:
An IPFIX Device uses a set of cooperating processes. Every Observation Point must be associated with at least one Metering Process, which captures packet headers, timestamps the packets, applies optional sampling and filtering, classifies packets into flows and maintains the Flow Records.

A flow is considered expired in three situations: no packets have been seen for a configurable time, with a minimum value of 0 seconds for immediate expiration, in which case the flow is reported as single-packet flows; the device runs short of resources such as memory; or, for a long-running flow, the metering process expires it on a regular, configurable basis.

The Exporting Process decides when and whether to export an expired flow, and sends it to one or more Collectors. The Collecting Process receives and decodes Flow Records, reports on lost records, and identifies the correct Control Information for each record. Packet selection may use sampling functions, with a rate of 1:1 meaning no sampling, and filter functions such as {Protocol == TCP, Destination Port < 1024}. The memo recommends selecting packets after their checksums have been verified.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device has one part that watches packets and keeps the tallies, one part that decides when to pack them up and send them, and one part at the far end that opens the packages and reads them. A tally group ends when no more packets arrive for a set time, when the device runs low on memory, or on a regular schedule, and a device that samples one packet in a hundred says so in the data.

sections.title: Control Information and Export
sections.content:
IPFIX exports two kinds of information. Control Information includes the flow definition, the selection criteria and the Templates that describe the data. The Data Stream carries the Flow Records. A Template is an ordered set of the Information Elements appearing in a Flow Record, together with their field sizes, and it lets the Collecting Process capture the structure and semantics of the records.

Templates bring three advantages: new fields can be added without changing the structure of the export record format; a Collector that does not understand a new field can ignore it but still interpret the record; and only the fields that are needed can be exported, which reduces data volume and possibly memory use, and lowers network load.

Control Information matters because the Collecting Process needs it to decode records and to understand the state of the Exporting Process. It should reach the Collector before the Flow Records it describes, and the export should be reliable; one way is to send it over a reliable transport. A device must use a congestion-aware transport for its Control Information and Data Stream. If the network does not guarantee reliability, at least the Control Information should use a reliable transport, while the Data Stream may use either. The named transports are SCTP, which supports both; TCP, reliable only; and UDP, unreliable only, for which operators need to keep traffic within their own administrative domains, for example on a dedicated network or Ethernet link.

When an IPFIX Device cannot observe all packets, for example when a Metering Process runs short of buffers, it should try to count the losses and report them to its Collectors.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending the tallies, the device sends a legend, called a Template, that says what each column means. The collector needs the legend to read the numbers at all, so the legend should come first and travel reliably. Several transport choices are named: one that is reliable, one that is not, and one that can be either. A device also has to use a transport that slows down when the network is busy.

sections.title: Collector Failure and Redundancy
sections.content:
The transport connection is pre-configured between the IPFIX Device and the Collector, because the protocol itself provides no way to configure the processes. Once connected, the device should set a keepalive, such as the TCP keepalive timeout or the SCTP HEARTBEAT interval, low enough to detect a Collector failure quickly. The RFC warns that extremely short keepalive intervals can wrongly abort the connection during transient congestion and add load when the link is otherwise idle.

With a single Collector, the device should stop sending Flow Records on a keepalive timeout and try to reestablish the connection. If failover is supported, backup sessions may be opened in advance and Control Information sent to them. Where secondary Collectors exist with priorities, the device opens a Data Stream to the one of next highest priority, sending Control Information too if that session was not opened in advance. Redundant Collectors can instead all receive the streams at once. Because IPFIX requires a congestion-aware transport, multicast is not an option for redundancy.

The memo also flags special situations that need clear classification guidelines: tunnel traffic such as GRE, IP-in-IP and L2TPv3; VPN traffic with overlapping private addresses; firewalls that drop packets by policy; and NAT devices that change the values of fields used as flow keys.
sections.plainLanguage: If the collector stops answering, the device notices through a regular heartbeat, stops sending, and can switch to a backup collector on its list. It cannot use a broadcast to reach several collectors at once, because the required transport does not allow it. The memo also notes that tunnels, VPNs, firewalls and address translation can confuse the way packets are grouped, so rules are needed for those cases.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An IPFIX system must provide different levels of protection on the wire, because different applications have different security needs. The IPFIX architecture must allow three levels. Host-based security means no protection, for when the transport is perceived as safe; this option is the most efficient and an IPFIX system must support it. Authentication-only gives data integrity and authenticity, and should provide replay attack protection, but no confidentiality. Encryption hides the data and must be used when the transport is unsafe. The RFC recommends using the transport layer's security functions, with TLS or DTLS, to meet these needs.

The system should allow end-point authentication so that either one-way or mutual authentication can be performed between the device and the Collector. If a device becomes overloaded, data may be lost, so Collectors should detect lost Flow Records and at least record how many. IPFIX-specific attacks include an attacker overwhelming the Collector with spoofed export packets or sending false reports; encrypting the control packets both ways helps the Collector identify and ignore spoofed data.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send the tallies unprotected, protected so nobody can change them, or fully encrypted. You choose based on how much you trust the path between the device and the collector. Both ends can also prove who they are to each other. If the device gets overloaded and records are lost, the collector should notice and count the missing ones, and encrypting both directions helps it ignore faked packets.

items.title: Metering Process
items.text: Observes packets at an Observation Point and builds Flow Records.

items.title: Exporting Process
items.text: Decides when to send and exports Flow Records and Templates to Collectors.

items.title: Collecting Process
items.text: Receives Flow Records and uses the Control Information to decode them.
